paper_title: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. However, existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover only a small number of web applications drawn from a few software categories, and restrict modality to text and vision. Live benchmarks broaden site coverage but sacrifice reproducibility, since pages and data drift between runs. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not meaningfully evaluate whether agents can understand and use audio and video content embedded within web tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce WebArena-Pro, a benchmark comprising 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, spanning distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. Across the evaluated agents, the best performance is achieved by both Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. The strongest GenericAgent configurations, Gemini 3.1 Pro omni and Gemma4 31B, both achieve 30.3%. Among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks, WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and the most comprehensive multimodal support to date. The benchmark treats audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, with dedicated actions for extracting information from each. WebArena-Pro runs each task in isolation and supports reproducible, parallel evaluation. Tasks are authored through a dedicated annotator interface, filtered by LLM-assisted triage, and finally validated by humans before release. Project page: https://webarena-pro.github.io

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Web agents driven by large language and vision-language models have moved quickly from synthetic clicking tasks toward broader browser work, including drafting and triaging messages, updating records in business applications, extracting insight from dashboards, editing media, and coordinating across heterogeneous tools [1, 6, 9, 12]. growing body of benchmarks has supported this progress, offering self-hosted web environments [23, 11], visually grounded tasks [14, 15], workplace-style Equal contribution. leads. <xing.han.lu@mail.mcgill.ca> and Siva Reddy <siva.reddy@mila.quebec>. Core contributors. Project Corresponding authors: Xing Han Lù Preprint. Figure 1: Overview of WebArena-Pro. (A) Domain heterogeneity. WebArena-Pro spans 20 self-hosted web applications across six domain categories (productivity, communication, analytics, business operations, design and media, and travel), each modeled on widely used service such as Notion, Slack, Spotify, Figma, or Airbnb. The full set of applications and their reference services are listed in Table 2. (B) Multimodal observation and action space. WebArena-Pro extends the agents observation space beyond text and vision to include audio and video. Embedded media sources are exposed to the agent through the accessibility tree, and agents invoke transcribe() and extract_frames() actions to convert temporal media into form usable during browser workflows. If the agents handle native audio and video processing, they invoke listen() and watch() actions. scenarios [7, 19], computer-use settings beyond the browser [18], and increasingly large task pools [2]. As models improve and the scope of attempted tasks widens, the design of the evaluation itself becomes central question. Despite this progress, current self-hosted web-agent benchmarks have limitations relative to the conditions needed for realistic and diverse measurement, as summarized in Table 1. First, prior self-hosted benchmarks cover only small number of web applications drawn from few software categories, which limits the heterogeneity of interfaces, workflows, and data models that an agent encounters during evaluation. Second, modality coverage is limited to text and vision, even though many real browser workflows involve temporal media such as audio and video embedded in web pages. parallel line of live benchmarks operates on real production websites [6, 20, 12], broadening site coverage beyond what self-hosted benchmarks offer. However, they sacrifice reproducibility, since pages, content, layouts, and policies drift between runs, making consistent evaluation across rollouts difficult. To this end, we introduce WebArena-Pro, benchmark for web agents that addresses these limitations. First, addressing the application coverage gap, WebArena-Pro spans 20 self-hosted web applications across six domain categories (productivity, communication, analytics, business operations, design and media, and travel), with applications modeled on widely used services such as Notion, Slack, Spotify, Figma, and Airbnb (Table 2 lists all 20). Second, addressing the modality gap, WebArena-Pro evaluates audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, exposing media sources through the accessibility tree and providing transcribe() and extract_frames() actions so that agents can incorporate temporal media directly into browser workflows. Third, addressing the reproducibility limitation of live benchmarks, WebArena-Pro runs each task in isolation against per-task seeded container state, supporting reproducible parallel evaluation that avoids drift between runs. Table 1: Comparing WebArena-Pro to existing reproducible benchmarks for web and computer-use agents. Isolation refers to per-task environment reset enabling contamination-free parallel execution. Human-curated indicates that tasks are authored or verified by humans rather than auto-generated. half-circle ( ) indicates partial support. WorkArena Suite combines WorkArena (33 templates instantiated to 19,912 instances) and WorkArena++ (682 compositional tasks, each sampling from thousands of valid configurations). OSWorld targets desktop applications rather than websites, with # Envs showing its 9 application domains. GymAnythings environments and tasks are LLM-generated at scale rather than human-curated. (cid:71)(cid:35) Benchmark # Envs Templates Instances Vision Audio Video Isolation Human-curated Tasks Modalities Eval & Execution WebArena [23] VisualWebArena [14] WebChoreArena [15] WorkArena Suite [4, 7] TheAgentCompany [19] OSWorld [18] Gym-Anything [2] WebArena-Pro (ours) 6 3 4 1 4 9 200 20 241 233 117 715 175 369 10,000+ 812 910 532 19,912 175 369 10,000+ 300 300 (cid:71)(cid:35) WebArena-Pro contains 300 tasks categorized by site coverage (204 single-site, 96 cross-site) and modality (221 text/vision, 79 audio/video), as detailed in Table 3. Unlike many prior benchmarks that generate many task instances from small set of templates, each task in WebArena-Pro has its own dedicated template, which yields more diverse evaluation  (Table 1)  . Tasks are authored through dedicated annotator interface and pass through two-stage filter, in which LLM-assisted triage flags candidates that appear infeasible or trivial and human reviewers make the final acceptance decision. This pipeline keeps task quality grounded in human judgment while using LLM assistance to scale the authoring process. Our contributions are as follows: Heterogeneous web coverage. We construct benchmark of 20 self-hosted web applications across six domain categories with distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. Audio and video as core web observations. We extend the web-agent action and observation space to temporal media, exposing audio and video sources through the accessibility tree and providing transcribe() and extract_frames() actions so that agents can use embedded media directly within browser workflows. Omni agents are provided with listen() and watch() actions. Reproducible, parallel evaluation. We run each task in isolation against per-task seeded container state, supporting reproducible parallel rollouts and avoiding drift between runs. Human-validated benchmark construction. We release task creation pipeline that combines an annotator interface, LLM-assisted infeasibility and triviality triage, and final human validation.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Self-Hosted Web Benchmarks. WebArena is the closest predecessor to WebArena-Pro. It introduced self-hosted benchmark for realistic web navigation over six web applications, with agents completing natural-language tasks by operating browser [23]. VisualWebArena [14] extended the setting to visually grounded tasks where success depends on understanding screenshots rather than only DOM text, and WebChoreArena [15] stressed long-horizon, tedious browsing patterns with self-hosted websites as well. While these benchmarks provide valuable foundations for realistic and reproducible web-agent evaluation, WebArena-Pro differs along three axes visible in Table 1. First, it covers 20 applications across six domain categories, the broadest application coverage among self-hosted web benchmarks. Second, it enforces per-task isolation by explicitly resetting application state between tasks. In contrast, these benchmarks retain state across tasks, so backend changes an agent makes while solving one task persist into the next and can contaminate later evaluations. Third, it authors each task as its own dedicated template. In contrast, these benchmarks instantiate many task instances from smaller template set (e.g., 241 templates for 812 instances in WebArena), which may lead to less diverse evaluation. 3 Enterprise Benchmarks. parallel line of work pushes toward workplace realism. WorkArena evaluates agents on common knowledge-work tasks in ServiceNow [7], and WorkArena++ extends this direction with compositional planning tasks and automatically generated ground-truth trajectories [4]. TheAgentCompany simulates small company across handful of internal services and introduces non-binary partial scoring [19]. These benchmarks emphasize enterprise workflows, long-horizon planning, and task composition. WebArena-Pro is complementary; rather than centering on one enterprise platform, it spans productivity, communication, analytics, business operations, design and media, and travel applications, while still retaining stateful authenticated workflows. Live and Computer-Use Benchmarks. Other benchmarks broaden the evaluation setting in different direction. Mind2Web studies generalization to real websites using collected human demonstrations [6], and OnlineMind2Web [20] considers live variant where the target websites may change over time. Live benchmarks improve ecological validity but make repeatability difficult, since pages, data, policies, and layouts can drift between evaluations. WebArena-Pro instead uses self-hosted applications and seeded data, which makes failures easier to reproduce and enables backend-state evaluation. Beyond the browser, computer-use benchmarks such as OSWorld [18] broaden the target from browsers to full desktop environments, and Gym-Anything [2] pursues different scaling axis by using LLMs to configure environments and auto-generate evaluators. WebArena-Pro instead focuses specifically on web software, where browser instrumentation and application-level reset can be made reliable enough for controlled experiments, and keeps task authoring human-validated. Multimodal Web Benchmarks. VisualWebArena showed that many web tasks require visual grounding and that text-only agents miss information that is obvious to humans [14]. WebArena-Pro follows this motivation and extends multimodal support beyond static visual content to include audio and video. To enable this, we add new actions to the action space of the agent, such as transcribe() and extract_frames(). The agent invokes transcribe() to convert an audio source to text and extract_frames() to sample representative frames from video source. The resulting transcripts are merged into the accessibility-tree observation as synthetic nodes, while extracted frames are returned as image content alongside the AXTree, so the agent perceives temporal media within the same observation structure it already uses for the rest of the page (Figure 1). Finally, VideoWebArena [13] keeps the original WebArena websites and adds external tutorial videos that agents must draw facts or skills from. Unlike VideoWebArena, WebArena-Pro builds its audio and video content into the 20 new self-hosted applications, so multimodal understanding is part of the environment itself.

sections.title: 3.1 Web Environments
sections.content: WebArena-Pro consists of 20 self-hosted web applications grouped into six domain categories, listed in Table 2. Each application runs as Docker container with seeded data and fixed login credentials, and is reachable at fixed local URL during evaluation. Before each task, the container state is reset to its seeded baseline, so changes made by an agent during one task do not persist into the next. Local hosting also fixes the application version and the database contents across runs, which removes the drift in pages, data, or policies. The six domains are productivity, communication, analytics, business operations, design and media, and travel. Within each domain the applications share broad task family, such as file management in productivity or dashboard analysis in analytics, but differ in interface conventions, authentication flows, and backend state schemas. NextCloud and MyDrive both store files, for example, but they expose distinct REST APIs, distinct folder and permission models, and distinct Document Object Model (DOM) structures, so an agent that has learned to operate one is not guaranteed to transfer to the other. This grouping is what allows WebArena-Pro to test transfer at the level of interface and backend conventions, rather than memorization of single product. Each application is modeled on familiar reference application, listed in the third column of Table 2, which names the workflow pattern reproduced rather than implying data or feature parity. 4 Table 2: The 20 self-hosted web applications in WebArena-Pro, grouped by domain. sections.title: 3.2 Tasks and Action Space
sections.content: A task in WebArena-Pro is specified by natural-language intent, one or more starting sites, an authenticated browser state, and an evaluation specification that determines success and partial credit (Section 3.3). WebArena-Pro contains 300 tasks, with each task authored as its own dedicated template  (Table 1)  . We categorize these tasks along two independent dimensions, namely site coverage and modality, with qualitative examples in Table 3. Along site coverage, 204 tasks are single-site and require the agent to complete workflow within one application, while 96 are cross-site and require the agent to coordinate between two or more applications, probing transfer across the interface and backend conventions of Section 3.1. Along modality, 221 tasks rely only on text and vision (text/vision tasks), while 79 are audio/video tasks that require information embedded in temporal media on page, such as the spoken content of podcast or the visual content of video. 5 Table 4: Qualitative rubric example from the NextCloud task configuration. The judge verifies whether the agent performed actions 1 and 2, and verifies outcomes 3 and 4 at each step. # Type Criterion 1 Action 2 Action 3 Outcome The agent viewed the Project Alpha Talk history. The agent typed Client Meeting Update as the name for new file. The content of the Client Meeting Update file states that the client meeting moved to next Thursday. 4 Outcome file named Client Meeting Update exists in the Nextcloud file directory. The default action space follows the BrowserGym convention [5], with element-targeted actions (click, fill, select_option, scroll) and navigation actions (goto, go_back). The observation space exposes each page as both structured accessibility tree and screenshot, enabling evaluation of text-only and vision-language agents under the same task specifications. To support audio/video tasks, we extend this default action space by surfacing audio and video sources as nodes in the accessibility tree and introducing four actions that operate on them (Figure 1). transcribe(url, start, end): Returns transcript of the audio segment from start to end (in seconds) using local Whisper model. extract_frames(url, n, start, end) (vision-language agents only): Returns evenly spaced frames from the video segment between start and end (in seconds). listen(url, start, end) (omni models only): Provides the audio segment from start to end (in seconds) as direct audio input to the model. watch(url, start, end, include_audio) (omni models only): Provides the video segment from start to end (in seconds) as direct video input to the model, optionally including synchronized audio. The agent invokes these actions when it judges that the audio or video content is needed for the task. The resulting transcripts and extracted frames from transcribe() and extract_frames() are returned as observations in the next step, with transcripts merged into the accessibility tree as synthetic nodes and frames returned as image content alongside the accessibility tree. For omni models, listen() and watch() allow the videos and audio to be sent with the accessibility tree and processed by the model as different modality.

sections.title: 3.3 Evaluation
sections.content: We evaluate each trajectory with rubric-based verifier. Every task is paired with small set of human-written criteria, tagged as [action] or [outcome]. Action rubrics measure whether the agent performed required steps, such as searching, filtering, or submitting form. Outcome rubrics measure whether the final state of the website or the final answer satisfies the request, and for question-answering tasks they include reference answer. We organize the rubrics of task into directed acyclic graph (DAG) with one rubric node per criterion. rubric node that depends on failed rubric node is counted as failed. task counts as success only when all of its rubric nodes pass, and we report the success rate as the fraction of tasks that succeed. Each grader decides whether rubric is satisfied, and each rubric node uses one or more graders. There are three kinds of graders. (1) Deterministic graders query the backend state of the website, for example whether booking exists, or look for required strings in the final answer of the agent. (2) Heuristic graders match patterns in the URLs the agent visited and the actions it took. (3) An LLM judge reads the trajectory and the rubric. When rubric has an unambiguous expected result, such as an exact name in the answer, deterministic grader decides whether the rubric node passes or fails on its own. Otherwise, the graders are applied in the order deterministic, heuristic, then LLM judge. If grader finds the rubric satisfied, the rubric node passes. If not, the next grader is tried, so that correct but unexpected solution can still be recognized. The LLM judge always comes last and makes the final decision, and it is the only grader for rubrics that cannot be verified from the backend state or the actions of the agent. 6 Figure 2: Qualitative example of Qwen3.6-27B agent trajectory in WebArena-Pro. Given single-site audio/video task on YT-Lite, namely In the video, Zener Diodes: The Unsung Heroes of Electronics, was there any act of soldering shown?, the agent first clicks the matching video thumbnail. On the video page, it invokes transcribe() to read the spoken content and extract_frames() to sample 10 representative frames. The transcript does not mention soldering, but the extracted frames at = 128.6 and = 144.7 show soldering iron, and the agent answers accordingly. The rubric verifier confirms passing trajectory.

sections.title: 3.4 Benchmark Construction
sections.content: Mock Data and Personas. Each application is shipped with seeded data so that tasks operate on realistic, non-empty state. Seed contents are application-appropriate and include documents, files, messages, calendar events, dashboards, listings, support tickets, and similar records, as well as the relations between them, such as channel memberships, file shares, and assignments. Each application is also seeded with one or more user personas, represented by credentials and pre-populated account state, so that tasks begin from an authenticated browser session. Task Creation Pipeline. Tasks are authored by an annotator team composed of the authors of this paper. Through dedicated annotator interface, an annotator writes the natural-language intent, selects the relevant sites, and drafts the evaluation rubric. Each candidate then undergoes an automated triage step that flags trivial tasks by running against an LLM-based agent and discarding those solved correctly on the first attempt. Tasks that pass triage are reviewed by second annotator on the live application, who confirms feasibility, finalizes the rubric items used for scoring, and confirms the difficulty label. Human validation is the gating step before task enters the released benchmark, and we do not release tasks that fail any of these checks.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Environment Setup. We evaluate agents by running each task in BrowserGym-compatible browser environment [5]. At the beginning of an episode, the benchmark starts fresh website container, waits for readiness, performs the required UI login, and navigates the browser to the task 7 start URL. The agent receives the natural-language intent, with the list of accessible websites for the task, and then acts in the browser until it calls done() or send_msg_to_user(), or reaches the maximum number of steps. Each task is limited to 50 browser actions. We report success rates using the benchmarks evaluator output. Modeling. We evaluate representative agent architectures paired with different language, visionlanguage, and omni models. Each agent has its own configuration and action space. For instance, GenericAgent [5, 7] is ReAct [22] agent that asks for chain-of-thought [17] and an action at each step. It uses the BrowserGym [5] harness to obtain observations and act on the web page. In our setup, GenericAgent instances receive the same task intent, browser observation, and high-level action space. GenericAgent instances operate on the accessibility tree, with screenshots augmented with Set-of-Mark [21]. They also use our WebArena-Pro custom action set, which is derived from the bid action set from BrowserGym, and augmented with done(), transcribe(), and extract_frames() actions, which respectively allow finishing the current task, transcribing audio segments, and extracting frames from video segments (Section 3.2). The action space for omni agents includes listen() and watch() instead, for direct modality interaction with both audio and video, respectively. OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code are evaluated via the Harbor [10] harness. These coding agents are provided with Playwright MCP and an augmented media MCP to allow transcribe() and extract_frames() functions. Playwright MCP handles the observation extraction and action execution on the browser. Detailed setup of these agents is given in Appendix A. We select twelve models as agent backbones: seven open-source models, including Qwen 3.5 9B, Qwen 3.6 27B, Qwen 3.8 27B, Qwen 3.8 Max Prime, Gemma4 26B A4B, Gemma4 31B [8], and Kimi 3.1 Pro. And five closed-source models, including Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, Gemini 3.1 Pro [16], Claude Opus 4.7 [3], Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT 6.1 Sol. We evaluate Gemini3.1 Pro as both text and an omni model. In the latter, it leverages raw audio and video files returned by the omni action space. For all models, we enable extended thinkingreasoning effort set to highand set the temperature to 1.0, following the recommendations of the respective model developers. We also cap the maximum number of tokens per step at 40k [5, 7] for GenericAgent runs. Rubric-based LLM Judge. We use Qwen 3.6 27B as the LLM judge, the last grader of the rubricbased verifier described in Section 3.3. We chose it over more expensive alternatives, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Kimi 2.6, because it agrees with human annotations nearly as well while being open-weight and cost-efficient (Appendix D). Metrics. We report task Success Rate (SR) as our primary metric, defined as the fraction of tasks for which every rubric passes under the rubric-based grader of Section 3.3. To capture partial progress on unsuccessful tasks, we also report partial-completion score that measures the fraction of rubric items passed per task, in Appendix B.2.

sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: Table 5 reports the success rate of each agent at 50-step budget. Both Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 achieves the highest overall SR at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.3%, and OpenCode with Qwen 3.8 Max Prime at 55.7%. Among GenericAgent configurations, Gemma4 31B and Gemini 3.1 Pro with omni support tie for the highest SR at 30.3%, while the Qwen models lag well behind at 5.0% and 15.7%. Even the strongest configuration leaves 38% of tasks without recorded success. These results demonstrate remaining headroom on WebArena-Pro, while highlighting the wide variation in performance across model and agent configurations. Performance also varies across domains, which shows the heterogeneity of the benchmark (Section 3.1). Communication yields the highest success rate for each of the five coding-agent configurations: Codex reaches 81.8%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi at 79.5%, Claude Code at 72.7%, OpenCode with Qwen at 70.5%, and OpenCode with Gemini at 65.9%. Codex and Claude Code tie for the lead in Productivity at 60.4%, while Claude Code leads in Design & Media at 65.3% and Business Operations at 57.1%. OpenCode with Kimi leads in Analytics at 68.8%. sections.title: 4.3 Site Coverage and Modality
sections.content: In Table 6, we report the success rate of each agent decomposed along two task axes, site coverage (single-site and cross-site) and modality (text/vision and audio/video). Cross-site tasks consistently yield lower success rates than single-site tasks, but the magnitude of the drop varies across agents. GenericAgent with Gemma4 31B shows the largest gap, falling from 38.2% on single-site tasks to 13.5% on cross-site tasks, drop of 24.7 percentage points. Codex leads on single-site tasks at 67.2%, but drops to 52.1% on cross-site tasks. Claude Code achieves the highest cross-site SR at 55.2%, compared with 65.7% on single-site tasks, yielding the smallest gap among the five coding-agent configurations at 10.5 percentage points. These results indicate that coordinating actions across multiple applications remains substantial challenge for current agents. The modality breakdown reveals more varied pattern. Within GenericAgent, audio/video tasks yield higher success rates than text/vision tasks for all models except Gemma4 26B A4B. This pattern may partly reflect the structured access provided by transcribe() and extract_frames(), which convert audio/video content into language and image inputs that these models can process. However, this advantage does not hold consistently across coding-agent configurations. OpenCode with Qwen 3.8 Max Prime and Kimi 3.1 Pro, Codex, and Claude Code perform worse on audio/video tasks than on text/vision tasks. OpenCode with Gemini 3.1 Pro instead shows small audio/video advantage of 1.9 percentage points. Codex and Claude Code tie for the highest SR in both modalities, achieving 64.3% on text/vision tasks and 57.0% on audio/video tasks. Thus, relative performance across modalities varies with the agentmodel combination.

sections.title: 4.4 Media Tools Ablation
sections.content: In this section, we report an ablation study on how much media access contributes to agent performance. We compare three configurations. (1) No media tools, where the agent cannot access audio or video content. (2) Tool-based media access (T/F only), where the agent calls transcribe() to obtain transcripts of audio and extract_frames() to obtain frames of videos. (3) Native omni access (W/L only), where the omni model Gemini 3.1 Pro receives the audio and video content directly as input. We evaluate all 79 tasks on AcidWave and YT-Lite, the two websites centered on audio and video. We also report results on subset of 43 tasks that cannot be solved from titles, 9 Table 6: Success rate (SR) of agents on WebArena-Pro at 50-step budget, decomposed along the two task axes of Section 3.2. sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Costs. The cost of each agent run depends on its architecture, harness, and underlying model. We report recorded API costs for 300-task evaluation, including retries and recovery runs but excluding hosting infrastructure. GenericAgent costs approximately USD 800 with Claude Opus 4.7. For the coding agents, recorded costs including agent inference are USD 386 for Claude Code with Opus 5.5, USD 166 for Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol, USD 689 for OpenCode with Qwen 3.8 Max Prime, and USD 340 for OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro. Judging with Qwen 3.6 27B through OpenRouter accounts for less than USD 4 per 300-task evaluation in these coding-agent runs. 10 Future work. The same self-hosted infrastructure that supports parallel evaluation can also serve as training environment, where the rubric-based verifier provides per-task reward signal for reinforcement learning or rejection sampling. The controlled environment also supports robustness studies that perturb the underlying web pages to test resilience to UI drift and prompt injection. Finally, expanding the action space to richer temporal modalities such as live voice and streaming video would let the benchmark track agents that move beyond static page interaction.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented WebArena-Pro, reproducible benchmark of 300 human-validated tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications spanning six domain categories. It treats audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, and runs each task in container isolation for reproducible parallel evaluation. Across twelve model backbones and four agent harnesses, the strongest agent, Claude Code with Opus 5.5 and Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol, reach only 62.3% success at 50-step budget, with cross-site tasks remaining harder than single-site ones, and media-access ablations demonstrate the importance of accessing audio and video content. These results indicate considerable headroom for progress on heterogeneous, multimodal web agents.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We note the following limitations to our work. Limited Temporal Interaction. Our action-space extension covers only prerecorded audio segments and discrete video frames, leaving richer temporal interaction modalities such as voice dialogue and live video streams to future work. Evaluation Comparability and Reliability. Our comparisons evaluate particular combinations of models, harnesses, and tool configurations. Performance differences cannot generally be attributed to model capability or harness design alone. shared 50-step budget also does not equalize computational resources: agents differ in token consumption, native tool use, observation frequency, and latency. Reported costs depend on provider pricing and cache utilization. Controlled comparisons across harnesses and repeated runs would strengthen conclusions about efficiency and reliability.

sections.title: C Failure Modes Analysis
sections.content: C.1 GenericAgent Failure Modes Across the eight models, failures involve incomplete workflows, unsuccessful navigation, incorrect selections, and premature termination. These patterns can overlap: an agent may repeatedly search for the wrong entity, exhaust its action budget, and leave required action unfinished. Model-level differences extend beyond trajectory length. Table 12 provides qualitative examples of models failures. Gemini 3.1 Pro has the lowest recorded failure rate. Its qualitative failure examples include omitted artifacts and incorrect target entities. Both Gemma models exhibit premature or empty finalizations in the reviewed examples. Qwen 3.6 27B solves more tasks than Qwen 3.5 9B, but still exhibits missed end-state actions and incorrect entity or value selections. Constraint tracking and evidence verification provide further explanations. An exact-constraint error occurs when the agent follows plausible but task-invalid condition, such as filtering Metabase category as Gadget instead of the required Electronics, or selecting flight without satisfying the requested price, date, or currency conditions. Verification failures arise when agents answer from titles, metadata, or nearby content without inspecting the requested video, song, image, or document. Table 13 illustrates these overlapping patterns. Figure 5 shows trajectory lengths for solved and unsolved tasks. The accumulation of unsuccessful runs at 50 steps highlights difficulty completing tasks within the available budget. Across the 2,400 Test runs, 878 of the 1,683 unsuccessful runs (52.2%) reached the 50-step limit. Short trajectories require different interpretation: they can represent either early failure or successful completion of short lookup or task supported by media tool. Trajectory length alone is therefore insufficient to diagnose premature termination. C.2 Coding Agents Failure Modes We analyze the five coding-agent configurations on the 300-task WebArena-Pro Test split: Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode with Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi 3.1 Pro, and Qwen 3.8 Max Prime. Table 14 illustrates representative failure modes. Across the 1,500 runs, 375 of the 633 graded failures (59.2%) received partial reward. Representative failures involve incomplete workflows or missing final state changes: agents prepared records without saving them, created files locally without placing them in the target application, or returned answers instead of updating the requested page. Stale references, obstructed clicks, and ineffective recovery further disrupted execution. Other observed failures involve cross-site coordination, visual event counting, and temporal localization despite successful media access. Short trajectories sometimes reflect clarification requests or explicit refusals rather than premature abandonment. Figure 6 shows trajectory lengths for solved and unsolved tasks across all five configurations. Of the 633 unsuccessful runs, 92 (14.5%) reached the 50-step limit. sections.title: D Judge Models
sections.content: We compare three candidate judges, Qwen 3.6-27B, Gemini-3.1 Pro, and Kimi 2.6, against human annotations. We select 50 tasks and collect one trajectory per task from each of six agent models, for 300 trajectories in total. Human annotators label each rubric of these trajectories as satisfied or not, and we report the rate at which each judge agrees with the human label. Table 15 shows the results. All three judges reach similar pooled agreement, between 89.5% and 90.6%. We choose Qwen 3.6-27B because it performs comparably to the other judges while being relatively small open-weight model. It can therefore be hosted locally at much lower cost, and its fixed weights keep the evaluation reproducible over time, unlike judges served only through commercial API.

sections.title: Peppermint
sections.content: YT-Lite seeded after the container creation. For most websites, the data is seeded when building the image; the container can then be built fast. Exceptions are made for ERP-Next, which initializes the containers with data when it starts. Media datasets. Some WebArena-Pro environments required media-heavy seed datasets that are stored outside Git and baked into Docker images at build time. For Acidwave, we created music catalog with CC-licensed MP3 assets and accompanying metadata, including title, artist, album, genre, duration, play counts, license, attribution, and source URL; the current seed references 50 unique audio files. For yt-lite, we used samples from FineVideo: videos were decoded locally, paired with generated thumbnails, and transcoded to 720p HEVC/H.265 for compression before being packaged in the yt-lite image. For Immich, we sampled photos from Open Images V7, assigned them across the admin and agent accounts, manually curated them to remove low-quality, inappropriate, duplicate, or privacy-sensitive images, and then baked the uploaded photos, thumbnails, database state, and ML cache into the final image.
